newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian dollar shaky ahead of U.S. Fed meeting.
newsitem.headline: Canadian dollar shaky ahead of U.S. Fed meeting.

text.p: The Canadian dollar, which rallied last week when the Bank of Canada surprised markets by raising interest rates, remains vulnerable to interest rate moves in the United States, economists said on Monday.
The dollar jumped almost one U.S. cent last week after the Bank of Canada stunned markets on Thursday with a 25-basis-point hike in its key bank rate.

The central bank said the rate rise, the first since February 1995, was needed to counter easing monetary conditions prompted by a one-month drop in the value of the Canadian currency against the U.S. dollar and other major currencies.

But the Bank's efforts to defend the Canadian dollar could be erased as soon as Wednesday if the Federal Reserve takes pre-emptive action to slow the U.S. economy at its 2-day Federal Open Market Committee meeting starting on Tuesday.

Analysts said the Fed was not expected to raise rates at this week's meeting, but that unexpectedly high U.S. growth in the third quarter could compel it to resume the monetary tightening it began three months ago.
The Fed hiked interest rates on March 25 in a move that led to a sudden drop in the Canadian dollar as investors moved cash into U.S dollar-denominated assets.

"If it really does look like the U.S economy is picking up steam again, you could see some downward pressure on the Canadian dollar over the next few weeks," said Doug Porter, senior economist with Toronto brokerage Nesbitt Burns.
Porter said that U.S non-farm payrolls, due to be reported on Thursday morning, would be the key economic data for Fed watchers.
"That report will go a long way to determining which direction the Canadian dollar takes," Porter said.
Economists said the wild card for the Canadian dollar rested with Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen.

They said the Canadian dollar could retreat back to its 1997 low of 71.30 U.S. cents if Thiessen did not follow through on the central bank's May monetary policy report announcing a move to a less stimulative monetary policy.
The Canadian dollar weakened to 72.42 U.S. cents on Monday from its opening level of 72.56 U.S. cents.

"Once the Bank of Canada begins to go on an absolute tightening phase, as opposed to last week's rebalancing of monetary conditions, then you should see the dollar catch a bit of a tailwind," Porter said.
Until the Bank makes that move, the Canadian dollar could continue to disappoint markets, Porter said.
